cleared.check: Line by line trace of a swap in a pool without a hook, from PoolManager.swap to the last delta written, for exact input and exact output in both directions.
cleared.result: swap rejects a zero amount and an uninitialized pool before anything else (src/PoolManager.sol:193-196). With hooks equal to address(0) beforeSwap returns the caller's amount unchanged and afterSwap returns a zero hook delta, because no permission bit is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:252-255, 298, 306). Pool.swap treats a negative amount as exact input and a positive amount as exact output at every place that branches on it (src/libraries/Pool.sol:313, 371, 453; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:61). For exact input the remaining amount rises toward zero by amountIn plus fee and the calculated amount grows by amountOut. For exact output the remaining amount falls by amountOut and the calculated amount falls by amountIn plus fee (Pool.sol:371-382). The final delta puts the specified amount in currency1 exactly when zeroForOne differs from exact input (Pool.sol:453-461), so the caller is debited the input currency and credited the output currency in all four cases. Both casts to int128 revert on overflow (Pool.sol:455, 459; src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:40-43). The protocol fee is booked to the input currency (PoolManager.sol:216, 238). _accountPoolBalanceDelta writes amount0 to currency0 and amount1 to currency1 for msg.sender (PoolManager.sol:226, 381-384). I found no step where a sign, an operand order or a cast gives the caller more than the pool math computed.

cleared.check: beforeSwap: the returned delta, the check that the swap type does not change, and the fee override word, including a hook that returns dirty upper bits.
cleared.result: The hook result must be exactly 96 bytes and start with the beforeSwap selector, otherwise the call reverts (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154, 259). The specified delta is read only when the address carries BEFORE_SWAP_RETURNS_DELTA_FLAG (Hooks.sol:266-270). It is added to the caller's amount with checked arithmetic, and the call reverts when an exact input amount becomes positive or an exact output amount becomes negative (Hooks.sol:273-278). An amount of exactly zero is allowed and makes Pool.swap return a zero delta without touching state (src/libraries/Pool.sol:320). The fee word is read only for a dynamic fee pool (Hooks.sol:263). parseFee assigns a full 32 byte word to a uint24 in assembly (src/libraries/ParseBytes.sol:16-21). The value is then used only through isOverride, which ANDs with 0x400000, and removeOverrideFlag, which ANDs with 0xBFFFFF, followed by a comparison with 1,000,000 (src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78, Pool.sol:303-305). Both masks are 24 bit constants, so upper bits supplied by the hook cannot reach the fee, whatever the compiler does with the assignment. Without the override bit the stored fee is used. A hook can set the fee of its own dynamic fee pool to any value from 0 to 100 percent, which is the recorded hook trust finding F-004 and does not reach pools without that hook.

cleared.check: afterSwap and the two _accountDelta calls: does the caller delta plus the hook delta always equal the pool delta, and can a cast or a packing step lose a value.
cleared.result: afterSwap takes the specified and unspecified parts of the beforeSwap return, adds the afterSwap return to the unspecified part with a checked int128 cast and a checked addition (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:295-303), places the two parts in currency order with the same rule that Pool.swap uses (Hooks.sol:307-309 against src/libraries/Pool.sol:453), and subtracts the hook delta from the swap delta (Hooks.sol:312). The subtraction works on sign extended halves and reverts when a half leaves the int128 range (src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:34-46). PoolManager.swap then credits the hook delta to the hook address and the remainder to msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:221-226). The pool was run with the adjusted amount, so the two accounts together receive exactly the pool delta and each must reach zero before unlock returns (PoolManager.sol:112). I transcribed these lines and ran 20,000 random combinations of direction, amount and hook delta. Caller plus hook equalled the pool delta in every accepted case, and the accepted and rejected cases matched the conditions written in test/CustomAccounting.t.sol:195-209.

cleared.check: Fee split between protocol and liquidity providers in each step, and the unchecked subtraction of the protocol share.
cleared.result: The swap fee is the LP fee when the protocol fee is zero and protocolFee + lpFee - floor(protocolFee * lpFee / 1e6) otherwise (src/libraries/Pool.sol:307, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:38-46). It equals the protocol fee only when the LP fee is zero, because the protocol fee field is 12 bits wide and capped at 1,000. In that case the whole step fee goes to the protocol. Otherwise the protocol receives floor((amountIn + feeAmount) * protocolFee / 1e6) and the rest goes to fee growth (Pool.sol:391-405). In 300,000 random step shapes over the whole price range, with liquidity from 0 to 2^127 and amounts up to 2^255, the protocol share never exceeded the step fee, so the unchecked subtraction at Pool.sol:395 did not wrap. The transcribed swap reproduced the protocol fee totals that test/PoolManager.t.sol:779-818 and test/DynamicFees.t.sol:286-318 expect in 12,000 random cases, including the rounding up when the LP fee is zero. Rounding favours liquidity providers over the protocol and never the swapper.

cleared.check: Rounding of every amount in a swap step, asking who gains if a result is off by one unit.
cleared.result: Exact input: the amount after fee is rounded down, the input needed to reach the target is rounded up, the fee on a full step is rounded up, the fee on a partial step is the whole remainder, and the output is rounded down (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:64-86). Exact output: the output to the target is rounded down, the input and the fee are rounded up (SwapMath.sol:88-104). The next price is rounded up when currency0 comes in and down when currency1 comes in, which moves the price less than the exact result for an input and more for an output (src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:31-120, 146-148, 175-177). Every rounding step is against the swapper. The transcription returned the values asserted in test/libraries/SwapMath.t.sol:69-180 for seven fixed vectors and the Swap event values asserted in test/DynamicFees.t.sol:156-279, test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol:94, test/PoolManager.t.sol:501-503 and 608.

cleared.check: Tick crossing, the sign of liquidityNet, the tick stored after a step, and the price limit bounds.
cleared.result: The loop asks the bitmap for the next tick at or below the current tick when zeroForOne and above it otherwise (src/libraries/Pool.sol:347-348, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:94-119), clamps the result to MIN_TICK and MAX_TICK (Pool.sol:351-356) and uses the nearer of that tick's price and the limit as the target (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:25-36). A crossing happens only when the step ends exactly on the price of an initialized tick. It flips both fee growth outside values with the updated growth of the input currency and applies liquidityNet with its sign reversed for zeroForOne (Pool.sol:413-428, 602-612). After a zeroForOne step that ends on a tick the stored tick is one below it (Pool.sol:431). I traced the following oneForZero swap, a liquidity add on each side of that tick and a donate from that state. Each of them treats the pool as sitting just below the tick, which agrees with the liquidity value the swap left. A zeroForOne limit must be above MIN_SQRT_PRICE and a oneForZero limit below MAX_SQRT_PRICE (Pool.sol:322-338), so a swap cannot cross MIN_TICK downward or reach the price of MAX_TICK. Addition of liquidityNet reverts above 2^128 - 1 (src/libraries/LiquidityMath.sol:10-19) and the per tick cap keeps the sum over all ticks below that bound (Pool.sol:165-173, 565-582). The transcription returned the next tick and the initialized flag asserted in 19 fixed cases of test/libraries/TickBitmap.t.sol:130-293 and met its two fuzz properties in 40,000 random cases.

cleared.check: Extremes of tick, price, liquidity, amount and fee, tested as solvency of one pool: can any sequence make a pool pay out more of a currency than it took in. This matters for every pool, because the PoolManager keeps no reserve per pool and a pool that overpays would draw on the balances of the others.
cleared.result: I wrote a third transcription of FullMath, UnsafeMath, BitMath, TickMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, LiquidityMath, TickBitmap, the position update and Pool.initialize, modifyLiquidity, swap and donate from the source text, with 256 bit wrapping where the source is unchecked or assembly. I checked it against the fixed values in the repository tests named in the other items. I then ran 8,000 random sequences of 5 to 40 operations: tick spacings 1, 10, 60, 200, 32767 and random, starting prices over the whole range including MIN_TICK and the ticks next to MAX_TICK, static fees from 0 to 100 percent, a per swap fee override in 40 percent of the swaps, protocol fees from 0 to 1,000 in both directions, liquidity up to 2^126, exact input and exact output amounts up to 2^255 with both the extreme and nearby price limits, and donations up to 2^126. After every operation, and after all positions were removed, the net amount the pool had received in each currency was at least the protocol fee accrued, in all 8,000 runs. 17 runs ended with a position that could not be removed. In each of them the fees paid into the pool in one currency exceeded 2^127 base units, which is the recorded finding F-005 and cannot happen for a token whose supply is below 2^127.

cleared.check: Zero liquidity in range: a swap step with liquidity 0 moves the price for free. Can that give the swapper tokens or damage positions.
cleared.result: With liquidity 0 the input to the target, the output and the fee are all 0, the step reaches its target and no fee growth is added (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:66-74, 84-90; src/libraries/Pool.sol:401). In the transcription a swap of 1e18 exact input through an empty range returned the delta (0, 0) and only moved the price and tick. Positions are not affected, because a later add or removal computes its amounts from the price and tick of that moment with the usual rounding (Pool.sol:206-237) and the solvency runs above include such moves. The free move matters for contracts that read a pool price as an oracle and for the gas cost recorded in the finding of this unit. It does not move funds in core.

cleared.check: Swap hook calls to an address that is a precompile, a system contract or an account without code: can the PoolManager be made to accept such a call during a swap.
cleared.result: callHook reverts unless the call succeeds and the return data is at least 32 bytes that start with the selector that was sent (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). An address without code returns nothing and fails this test. beforeSwap also needs exactly 96 bytes (Hooks.sol:259) and afterSwap with the return delta flag exactly 64 bytes (Hooks.sol:166). A contract that returns its input unchanged passes the selector test but returns the whole call data, which is longer than 96 bytes for beforeSwap and longer than 64 bytes for afterSwap, so it cannot act as a swap hook that returns deltas. It can only pass as an afterSwap hook without the return delta flag, where the return value is ignored (Hooks.sol:163). A failed hook call reverts the whole swap, so a side effect in the callee does not survive. Such a pool is one that somebody chose to create with that address as hook, and pools without a hook never make these calls.

cleared.check: A native asset that also answers as an ERC-20 at some address: can sync, settle and take, in any order, credit one payment twice or credit more than was paid. Exhaustive search over a model of src/PoolManager.sol:279-297 and 349-364.
cleared.result: I modelled the PoolManager balance, the synced currency, the synced reserves, the two deltas and the attacker's wallet, with operations sync(0), sync(face), settle with value, settle without value, take in each currency, a transfer through the face and a native transfer that reaches the PoolManager without a call. I searched every sequence of up to 6 operations with amounts 1, 2 and 3. When the face reports the native balance one to one, no sequence left the attacker better off. The guard at PoolManager.sol:356 blocks the only order that would count a value twice. When the face reports floor(native / S) for S above 1, the best sequence gained S - 1 base units per round of sync and settle, and it needs native value to arrive without a call while the face is synced. On Arc the USDC contract at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 returns decimals 6 and its balanceOf for the PoolManager equalled floor(eth_getBalance / 1e12) at blocks 0x1f14a00, 0x1f14a63 and 0x1f14a79, with remainders of 930109466545, 178438878313 and 971982015932 base units. S is therefore 1e12 there and one round can gain less than 0.000001 USDC. I did not test whether native USDC can reach the PoolManager without a call on Arc, and I did not query the one to one property on Celo and Polygon again. For those two I rely on the earlier findings F-023 and F-008.

cleared.check: Slot0 packing: field offsets, mask widths, sign handling of the tick and the effect of dirty upper bits passed to a setter.
cleared.result: The four fields sit at bit offsets 0, 160, 184 and 208 with widths 160, 24, 24 and 24, so they end at bit 232 and do not overlap (src/types/Slot0.sol:33-38). MASK_160_BITS is written with 42 hex digits, two of them leading zeros, and equals 2^160 - 1. Every setter ANDs the new value with its mask before the shift and clears only its own field in the packed word (Slot0.sol:66-93). The tick getter sign extends from 24 bits (Slot0.sol:47-51). I transcribed the eight functions into Python and ran 200,000 random cases in which each setter received a full 256 bit value. Every getter returned the input truncated to the field width, the top 24 bits of the word stayed unchanged, and the order of the setters did not change the result. cleared.check: BalanceDelta and BeforeSwapDelta packing and unpacking, and the arithmetic on packed deltas.
cleared.result: toBalanceDelta shifts amount0 left by 128 bits and masks amount1 to 128 bits, so sign extension bits of a negative amount1 cannot reach amount0 (src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:14-18). amount0 is read with sar 128 and amount1 with signextend 15 (BalanceDelta.sol:61-71). add and sub split both operands, add or subtract the halves as 256 bit numbers and pass each half through SafeCast.toInt128, which reverts when the result leaves the int128 range (BalanceDelta.sol:20-46, src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:40-43). A carry from the low half therefore cannot enter the high half. BeforeSwapDelta uses the same layout with the specified amount in the high half (src/types/BeforeSwapDelta.sol:9-37). A Python transcription returned the inputs for 200,000 random int128 pairs and for the extreme pairs. The hook delta that reaches these functions is a full word chosen by the hook, and both halves are valid int128 values by construction, so no bit pattern is out of range.

cleared.check: Fee fields: LP fee bounds and flag bits, the two 12 bit protocol fee halves, the combined swap fee and the unchecked subtraction of the protocol share.
cleared.result: MAX_LP_FEE is 1,000,000, which is below 2^20, so a valid fee never touches bit 22 (override flag 0x400000) or bit 23 (dynamic flag 0x800000) (src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:15-25). A pool is dynamic only when the fee field equals 0x800000 exactly (LPFeeLibrary.sol:30-32). isValidProtocolFee masks the low and the high 12 bits and compares them with 1001 and 1001 << 12 (src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32). I checked the function against the plain rule for one seventh of all 2^24 inputs. calculateSwapFee masks both inputs and returns p + l - floor(p * l / 1e6) (ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:38-46). For every p from 0 to 1000 and a grid of l up to 1,000,000 the result stayed at or below 1,000,000 and was at least p and at least l, and it equalled p only when l was 0. The step fee is at least amountIn * swapFee / (1e6 - swapFee) rounded up, or the whole remainder on a partial step (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:72-82, 104), so the protocol share floor((amountIn + feeAmount) * p / 1e6) cannot exceed it and the unchecked subtraction at src/libraries/Pool.sol:391-396 cannot wrap. cleared.check: Hook return data: which bits of the returned words the PoolManager uses, and whether dirty bits in a hook answer can change a value outside that hook's own pool.

The selector is compared as bytes4, so only the first four bytes of the first word count (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152). The fee word is used only for a dynamic fee pool and only through an AND with 0x400000, an AND with 0xBFFFFF and a comparison with 1,000,000 (Hooks.sol:263, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78, src/libraries/Pool.sol:303-305), so bits above bit 23 are dropped whatever the compiler does with the assembly assignment, and a returned dynamic flag makes the fee fail validation. The delta word is split into two int128 halves and applied with checked arithmetic (Hooks.sol:266-279, 295-313). The hook is credited exactly what the caller is debited (src/PoolManager.sol:181-183, 224-226). Every value a hook can influence stays inside the pool that names that hook. cleared.check: Hook flag bits and the validity rule: do the 14 flags overlap, does operator precedence give the intended test, and which special addresses pass the rule.
cleared.result: The 14 flags are the single bits 13 down to 0 and ALL_HOOK_MASK is 2^14 - 1 (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:27-47). In Solidity the bitwise AND binds tighter than the comparison, so hasPermission tests (address & flag) != 0 and the last line of isValidHookAddress tests (address & mask) > 0 (Hooks.sol:126, 337-339). I enumerated all 16,384 low bit patterns. With a static fee exactly 5,183 are accepted, which is 3^4 * 2^6 - 1: each of the four return delta bits needs its action bit, and the all zero pattern is refused. The zero address is accepted only with a static fee, and an address without flags only with the dynamic fee value (Hooks.sol:124-126). The fixed cases in test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol:940-990 agree, including the refusal of an address whose only set bit is bit 14. Low addresses that pass include 0x10, 0x64, 0x100 and 0x101. A precompile or a codeless account at such an address cannot answer with 32 bytes that start with the hook selector, so the hooked action of that pool reverts (Hooks.sol:152-154). That is the recorded hook trust finding F-004 and needs victims to choose a pool with that hook address. The identity precompile at 0x04 echoes its input and would pass the selector test, and its address carries bit 2 without bit 6, which the rule refuses (Hooks.sol:112).

cleared.check: Do the 21 networks execute the bit level instructions of this unit as the code expects, and what do codeless and precompile targets return to a transfer shaped call.
cleared.result: I sent one 980 byte creation payload with eth_call and no to address to the RPC endpoint of each network in state/networks.json on 2026-11-22. It returns 28 words: SIGNEXTEND 15 and 2 on values with dirty upper bits, SAR 128, the BalanceDelta pack of (-5, -7), a Slot0 tick read, the delta slot hash, TLOAD before and after TSTORE, SDIV and SMOD of MIN_TICK by 60, a BYTE table lookup, SHL, SHR by 256, MULMOD by 2^256 - 1 and a 160 bit AND. It also makes four calls with the 68 byte calldata of transfer(address,uint256) and a 32 byte output area at memory 0. All 21 networks returned the 28 expected words. A codeless address and the ecrecover precompile at 0x01 return success with empty return data and leave memory word 0 unchanged. Under src/types/Currency.sol:64-74 a take in currency 0x01 or in a codeless currency therefore counts as paid and moves nothing, which only debits the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295), and a take in currency 0x02 or 0x04 reverts. sync decodes a 32 byte result, so it reverts on empty data and reads a constant on 0x02 and 0x04, and the difference between sync and settle is then zero (Currency.sol:94, PoolManager.sol:358-360). SOL-2026-7 needs a variable that is used to compute memory or storage addresses, is reassigned in a loop or branch, and yields two addresses with different constant offsets that coincide at run time, followed by a load or an equal store. Those functions never read back what they stored and never store a value twice, so neither affected optimizer step has anything to replace. Every other block derives its addresses from constants or from a pointer assigned once (src/types/Currency.sol:57, src/libraries/Position.sol:55, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:142, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:67-73, src/libraries/Pool.sol:547). The Solidity team states that the condition cannot be decided from Solidity source because it depends on the intermediate Yul code. The flag is set only at line 107, cleared only at line 113, and unlock reverts when it is already set (105). ERC-6909 balances change only in transfer, transferFrom, _mint and _burn with checked arithmetic (src/ERC6909.sol:25-48, 79-89). From I1 to I7 it follows that for every currency id the PoolManager balance stays at or above pool reserves plus claims plus accrued protocol fees, as long as four properties of the chain and the token hold: T1, balanceOf(PoolManager) of a currency changes only by transfers to or from the PoolManager and by the transferred amount; T2, no second currency id draws on the same balance in another unit; T3, msg.value arrives in full; T4, transient storage is one store per transaction that follows call and revert semantics. In every completed run the attacker's wallet did not grow, the victim paid exactly its amount and kept its claim. cleared.check: A stale sync: sync needs no lock, and its two slots are the only settlement state that can outlive an unlock. What can a party gain from a sync left behind inside one transaction, and what would follow if a network failed to wipe transient storage between transactions.
cleared.result: unlock ends with the flag false and the counter zero or it reverts (src/PoolManager.sol:105-113), so after any successful call the lock flag and all deltas are zero and only the synced currency and reserves can remain (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-32). The model treats a whole sequence as one transaction and found no gain from a sync that survives between unlocks. The effects that remain are these. A later settle with msg.value reverts with NonzeroNativeValue until someone calls sync again (src/PoolManager.sol:356). collectProtocolFees for that ERC-20 reverts (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52). The next settle without a new sync credits the caller with every rise of that balance since the stale sync, which inside one transaction can only be the caller's own payment or an inflow it triggered. If a network kept transient storage across transactions, the same reading gives two consequences and no more: native payers who do not call sync first would revert until the slot is reset, and a party could leave a sync in one transaction and book unsolicited inflows, such as a positive rebase, in a later one. Deposits of other users are not exposed, because every ERC-20 settle resets the slot and every payer that follows the interface comment calls sync first (src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:165-171). A leak of the lock flag or of a delta across transactions would be a different and total failure, and the code gives no path to it under call and revert semantics.

cleared.check: Arc: the CallFrom precompile at 0x1800000000000000000000000000000000000003 starts a call on behalf of Memo and Multicall3From. Does that inner call run with transient storage of its own, which would separate PoolManager deltas from payouts inside one unlock, and can a contract in the middle of a transaction use it to act as another account at the PoolManager.
cleared.result: No to both, in the main branch of the client. The precompile builds an ordinary CALL input with the chosen sender as caller and zero value (call_from.rs, decode_child_call). ArcEvm::init_subcall rejects static context and value, rejects a substituted sender that is neither the calling helper nor the transaction signer, and then pushes the child through the same frame stack and the same journal as every other call, with a journal checkpoint taken from that journal (evm.rs, init_subcall and complete_subcall). A child frame on the same journal sees and writes the same transient storage as its parent, so the lock flag, the deltas and the counter of the PoolManager stay one consistent store (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:12-34). Memo passes msg.sender as the sender (Memo.sol, memo), which closes the part the stablecoin unit left unread. A contract that is not the signer therefore cannot reach the PoolManager as someone else, and the ERC-6909 functions that trust msg.sender (src/ERC6909.sol:25-64) keep their meaning. I read the main branch and did not confirm which release mainnet runs, and I did not read revm itself for where transient storage lives; the stablecoin unit did.

cleared.check: Sweep of all 18 precompiles with the PoolManager as sender: empty calldata with zero value and with 1 ETH (P1), transfer(address,uint256) with zero and 1e18 (P2), balanceOf(PoolManager) (P3) and all ten IHooks selectors with well-formed arguments (P5). Follow-up on each target that did not revert.
cleared.result: No precompile yields a credit or an unpaid outflow. ECRECOVER and P256VERIFY return empty data: take succeeds and moves nothing while the caller is debited, and sync reverts because the Solidity decoder needs 32 bytes, so no credit can arise. SHA256, RIPEMD160 and IDENTITY return 32 bytes or more that depend only on the input, so the value read at sync equals the value read at settle and paid is zero; their answer to transfer is a digest or the echoed calldata, never the word 1, so take reverts. The other precompiles fail on the input lengths the PoolManager can produce. ETH sent to a precompile address with a native take stays there and the caller owes it. The sync results on the existing mainnet deployment (reverts for 0x01, 0x100 and an empty address, succeeds for 0x02, 0x03, 0x04) agree with this reading of the source; I used them as a behavioural reference and did not compare code.

cleared.result: ETH and WETH9 are separate balances. There is one sync slot, each sync overwrites both transient values, and a credit is the measured rise since the latest sync, so one transfer in is credited once under one id. Each take sends at most what it debits under the id named. Over all ids that share a balance, credits minus debits equal the real change. A native payment cannot be counted under an ERC-20 id because settle rejects msg.value while an ERC-20 is synced, settle and settleFor are the only payable functions, and sync(address(0)) followed by a later sync re-reads the balance. cleared.check: Opcode and call semantics the PoolManager relies on, read in the Osaka execution specification: transient storage lifetime and rollback, value transfer order, static context, return data after failed calls, gas forwarding and precompile dispatch.
cleared.result: Transient storage is created per transaction and rolled back with the frame, value moves before callee code runs and is undone on failure, a failed or underfunded call returns 0 with empty return data, and the callee receives at most 63/64 of the gas. The source handles each case by reverting: a failed native or token transfer reverts with a wrapped error, a failed hook call reverts, and a failed balanceOf reverts through the decoder. No path continues after a failed external call, so the gas rule can make an operation fail and cannot make it half succeed.

cleared.check: Known weaknesses of mainnet execution clients, precompiles and system contracts from the last two years: could an ordinary account use any of them against funds in the PoolManager.
cleared.result: The incidents I found are liveness and consensus faults: the Reth state root stall of 2025-09-02, Nethermind nodes rejecting a canonical block at the Fusaka fork, and client fixes for MODEXP in Geth and P256VERIFY in Besu that the Fusaka retrospective lists. A node that stalls or rejects a block does not execute a different result for an included transaction, and settlement in core is atomic inside one transaction. The PoolManager calls a precompile only when a caller names one as currency, hook or recipient, and the sweep shows those calls give the caller nothing. I did not search vendor advisory databases one by one, and I did not find a published mainnet bug in TSTORE, TLOAD or CALL handling.

cleared.result: No departure from Ethereum was found. call_impl applies the 63/64 rule, the 2300 stipend and the depth limit and reports success only for status Success. pre_call moves value for CALL and CALLCODE inside a pushed state version, and post_call rejects that version on any failure, which restores balances, storage and transient storage. cleared.check: Whether the 8 MB memory cap per transaction (MIP-3) can break a PoolManager path that copies return data, or freeze a withdrawal.
cleared.result: No. The PoolManager copies hook return data and revert data in full (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:140-149, src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119) and copies 32 bytes after a token transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:73). A callee that returns more than the remaining memory makes the PoolManager frame halt, which reverts the call. Only a hook or token chosen for the pool can do this, and that case is F-004. A removal in a pool without such a hook uses a few hundred bytes of memory.

cleared.result: The opcode bodies are the revm handlers with accounting wrappers, so results are those of Ethereum Prague. The changed rules are fail-closed for the PoolManager. A child that receives less gas or exceeds its resource share reverts, and the PoolManager reverts on a failed native transfer, token transfer, hook call or unlock callback (src/types/Currency.sol:51-53 and 82-86, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:137). No path treats a failed call as success. The extra 23,000 gas stipend on value calls cannot pay computation, and the PoolManager forwards all gas anyway.

cleared.check: A1 from the node source: does transient storage end with the transaction, including after an error or a panic, and does the KeylessDeploy sandbox share it.
cleared.result: Yes for the transaction boundary and no for the sandbox. Every transaction ends with the journal finalize step that clears transient storage, and the panic recovery path calls the same step. The sandbox database reads accounts and storage from the parent journal state and has its own journal. Together with the cycle 1 reading of the Monad client this answers the open question on transient storage for chains 143 and 4326.

cleared.check: Whether an attacker can inflate the SALT bucket that holds a victim's storage slot until a zero to nonzero write there becomes unaffordable, given that the bucket index comes from a fixed-seed hash.
cleared.result: Not on the normal path. A bucket doubles when it is more than 80 percent full, so reaching multiplier 2^k needs about 205 times 2^k entries in that bucket, each paying 20,000 times (multiplier minus 1) storage gas at the multiplier in force. The total is about 2.7 million times 4^k gas. Multiplier 1,024 costs the attacker about 2.8 ETH at the current base fee and adds 20.5 million gas, about 0.00002 ETH, to one write by the victim. A write that exceeds the 10 billion gas transaction limit needs a multiplier near 500,000 and about 740,000 ETH. A removal mostly clears slots or rewrites nonzero slots, and the recipient of a payout can choose an address that already holds the token. The figures are computed from the documented rule, and the value of NUM_KV_BUCKETS was not read.

cleared.check: Whether a call that the PoolManager issues can match a MegaETH call interceptor (Oracle sendHint, KeylessDeploy, MegaAccessControl, MegaLimitControl) and produce a synthetic success.
cleared.result: No. Each interceptor requires the target address and a specific four-byte selector. The PoolManager can address a system contract only as a currency or as a hook, with transfer, balanceOf, an IHooks selector or empty calldata. None of these matches, the call falls through to the contract code, and the code reverts on all of them. The hook route is closed earlier, because the addresses end in 1 to 6 and fail isValidHookAddress (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:111-120).

cleared.check: Whether gas detention or disableVolatileDataAccess can be imposed on another user's PoolManager transaction.
cleared.result: No. Detention state is reset at the start of each transaction and applies to the transaction that made the volatile read. The access control switch covers the caller's frame and its descendants. A third party is in neither position for a victim's transaction unless the victim's pool uses that party's hook or token, which is F-018. Since REX4 the cap is relative, so a transaction can always spend 20 million compute gas after the read.

cleared.check: Known weakness: the Spearbit finding that DELEGATECALL to the staking precompile credited stake without moving MON, and its STATICCALL variant. Can an ordinary account use the precompile against PoolManager funds today.
cleared.result: No. The fix rejects every message whose kind is not CALL or whose flags are nonzero before dispatch, and the STATICCALL probe from the PoolManager address fails. The PoolManager never issues DELEGATECALL (no use in src outside tests) and cannot send a staking selector. The precompile takes funds only from msg.value of its caller.

cleared.check: Known weaknesses in the reserve balance rule: the Code4rena finding on EIP-7702 delegation status that let a sender stall block proposals for free, the testnet crash of 2025-09-27 from relaxed balance merging, and the three bugs described by Category Labs. Can any of them be used against funds in the PoolManager.
cleared.result: No path was found. All of them concern whether a sender can pay its fee and whether consensus and execution agree on that. Their effect is a stalled or halted chain, which delays every user alike and moves no balance. The execution check skips accounts whose final code is contract code, so the PoolManager is never the account under test. A user who adds MON and ends below the reserve can have the deposit reverted when the emptying exception does not apply, and a payout only raises the recipient's balance.

cleared.check: Known weaknesses: the BlockSec findings on MegaEVM (unbounded TSTORE, cheap KZG, KZG gas cost crash, costly opcode loops) and the REX4 audit fixes. Can an ordinary account use them against funds in the PoolManager.
cleared.result: No path was found. Each is a way to load or crash the node or to escape a resource limit. The PoolManager writes transient storage at fixed slots and at one slot per account and currency (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41), which a caller can multiply only at its own gas cost, and the effect is on node memory. Three of the four BlockSec findings are marked confirmed without a stated fix, so node availability under these loads stays an operator matter. Only the report index was read.

The 0x0100 case is the one cycle 1 recorded, and it also exists on any chain with the P256 precompile.

cleared.result: No. Two calls to 0x0809 inside one execution returned the same value (0x495c881c and 0x495c881c), while separate executions about a second apart returned 0x495c8830 and 0x495c8846. sync and settle run in one transaction because the synced currency is transient (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-38), so paid is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). take under this id reverts, because the 32 byte answer is not 1 (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). This confirms the cycle 1 clearance with a measurement inside one execution.

cleared.check: Do the HYPE bridge 0x2222...2222, CoreWriter 0x3333...3333, the CoreDepositWallet, a token system address and the system interest address accept any PoolManager call shape other than the native payout already recorded in F-021?
cleared.result: No. The bridge accepts empty calldata with or without value and reverts on transfer, balanceOf and all ten hook selectors. CoreWriter reverts on all fifteen shapes. The CoreDepositWallet reverts on all fifteen, and its transfer function names the reason: Caller is not the system address. 0x2000000000000000000000000000000000000077 and 0x5000000000000000000000000000000000000000 have no code, so a take to them is an ordinary transfer by the PoolManager that the caller pays for, and a take that names them as currency moves nothing and debits the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297).

cleared.check: Which special addresses pass the hook address check, and can the PoolManager be made to call them inside a pool action with an accepted answer (P5)?
cleared.result: Four pass Hooks.isValidHookAddress (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127): WHYPE, EntryPoint v0.6, 0x0800 and 0x0810. WHYPE has the afterInitialize flag and its fallback returns no data, so callHook reverts with InvalidHookResponse and initialize reverts (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154, src/PoolManager.sol:141). EntryPoint v0.6 has the beforeInitialize flag and reverts on the selector, so initialize reverts. The two precompiles are covered above. Every other special address fails the flag check.

cleared.check: Can a native payout to WHYPE, whose fallback wraps the value for the sender, leave the PoolManager owing native HYPE that it no longer holds, or give the caller a WHYPE credit it did not pay for?
cleared.result: No. take(address(0), WHYPE, x) debits the caller x of the native id before the call (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295) and WHYPE credits the PoolManager x WHYPE. If the caller had synced WHYPE first, settle credits it x under the WHYPE id (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364). The caller then holds a debit of x native and a credit of x WHYPE and must clear both before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112). Whichever way it clears them, the native balance and the native amounts owed fall together and the WHYPE balance and amounts owed rise together. This is an in place wrap paid by the caller.

cleared.check: stHYPE and wstHYPE: can one deposit be credited under both currency ids, can an ordinary account raise the stHYPE balance of the PoolManager inside its own sync window, and does rounding between the two units pay out more than a dust amount?
cleared.result: No to all three. The synced currency is one transient slot, so only one measuring window is open at a time and a second sync replaces the first (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). Each window credits the rise of one balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), and both balances rise only when shares arrive: the stHYPE rate depends on block.timestamp alone between rebases (stHYPE.sol lines 495 to 513), mint and burn keep the rate (lines 244 to 256), and rebase is role gated. Every take is debited in full under the id it names (src/PoolManager.sol:294). The sum of credits therefore never exceeds the shares paid in. Rounding: an stHYPE transfer moves floor(amount times shares per unit) of 24 decimal shares and wstHYPE moves multiples of 1e6 shares, so one settle can be off by at most one base unit of either token, far below the gas cost of the call. The effects that remain need the issuer and are in the stHYPE finding.

cleared.check: Recheck of assumption A3 on 2026-11-22: does native HYPE now have an ERC-20 face or a linked EVM contract, and is any HyperCore token linked to the PoolManager, to WHYPE or to a system address?
cleared.result: No. spotMeta returns evmContract null for HYPE (index 150). Of 194 linked tokens no two share an address and none points at the PoolManager, WHYPE, the bridge, CoreWriter or a 0x20 address. WHYPE remains a plain wrapper whose code has no path that reads another account's native balance.

cleared.check: Assumption A1 for system transactions, including the AQAv2 ones whose sender is the CoreDepositWallet or the treasury address: can an unlock flag, a delta or a stale sync written in one transaction be read by the next transaction of the block?
cleared.result: No, on the evidence of the maintained archive client. It runs every system and signed transaction through one transact call (src/node/evm/executor.rs lines 192 to 213), and the revm fork it pins clears transient storage in commit_tx, discard_tx and finalize and restores it on checkpoint revert (journal/inner.rs lines 97 to 180 and 461 to 476). The client recovers any 20 byte sender from the s value, so the AQAv2 senders are covered, and it rejects a block whose gas used, receipts root or logs bloom differs from the header written by the validator node (src/node/consensus/reth_copy.rs lines 27 to 45). Lock, CurrencyDelta, CurrencyReserves and NonzeroDeltaCount (src/libraries/Lock.sol:10-27, CurrencyDelta.sol:28-41, CurrencyReserves.sol:21-38, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:12-34) therefore start each transaction at zero. This closes the gap the critic named for the replay client. The limit of the evidence: a header comparison shows a difference only if some past transaction depended on leaked transient state, and the validator binary itself is closed.

cleared.check: Can system transactions crowd signed transactions out of a block and so delay a liquidity removal, given that an ordinary account can trigger them through HyperCore transfers?
cleared.result: No. The archive client adds gas to the block total only for transactions that are not system transactions (src/node/evm/executor.rs lines 225 to 227) and checks each signed transaction against the remaining block gas without them (lines 196 to 206). A removal needs no loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238) and fits a fast block.

cleared.check: Does the PoolManager address have a HyperCore account, a HyperCore balance or the big block flag, and can a third party set any of these in a way that changes how the PoolManager behaves on the EVM?
cleared.result: No account exists: spotClearinghouseState returns no balances, userRole returns missing and preTransferCheck returns userExists false. A third party can create the account and fund it by sending HyperCore assets to the address, which changes nothing on the EVM. The big block flag and every HyperCore action need a signature of the account or a CoreWriter call by it, and the PoolManager can make neither (cycle 1 clearance on CoreWriter, rechecked: CoreWriter reverts on every PoolManager call shape).

cleared.check: Opcode differential for the opcodes and call patterns the PoolManager relies on: do TSTORE, TLOAD, SSTORE, SLOAD, MCOPY, KECCAK256, LOG, BALANCE, EXTCODESIZE, SELFBALANCE, CALL with and without value, STATICCALL, RETURNDATASIZE, PUSH0 and CREATE cost what they cost on Ethereum, and does the client change any of them?
cleared.result: They cost the same in 23 measured snippets, to the unit of gas. The archive client uses revm's mainnet instruction table and replaces only BLOCKHASH for blocks below 243,538 (src/evm/api/mod.rs lines 33 to 43). Core does not use BLOCKHASH. The measured differences are confined to seven precompiles that core never calls.

cleared.check: Did the November 2026 hard fork move HyperEVM past Cancun or enable EIP-7702, which would let code at a hook address change (A7)?
cleared.result: No. The fork is a precompile repricing. Both spec ids of the archive client map to revm's CANCUN (src/evm/spec.rs line 17), the Prague precompile addresses 0x0b to 0x11 and 0x0100 still answer like empty accounts, and the HyperEVM docs page still states Cancun without blobs.

cleared.check: Does any file under src outside src/test read the chain id, block fields, the transaction origin, the gas price or external code, or contain a hardcoded address, so that the code could behave differently on HyperEVM than elsewhere?
cleared.result: No. A search of src outside src/test for chainid, block., blockhash, timestamp, coinbase, basefee, prevrandao, gasprice, origin, selfbalance, extcode, create, selfdestruct, delegatecall and for 20 byte literals finds only the delegatecall guard (src/NoDelegateCall.sol:19-25) and address masks. The raw external calls are the native payout and the ERC-20 transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:48 and 73) and the hook call (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134); the high level calls are unlockCallback (src/PoolManager.sol:110) and balanceOf (src/types/Currency.sol:94 and 102).

cleared.check: Can an EntryPoint address used as currency draw on any balance that belongs to other users, since both EntryPoints answer balanceOf(PoolManager) and accept native value from the PoolManager?
cleared.result: No. The EntryPoint deposit of the PoolManager rises only when native value is sent for it. If the PoolManager sends it through take, the caller is debited the native amount (src/PoolManager.sol:294). A credit under the EntryPoint id can be minted as a claim and can never be paid out, because transfer(address,uint256) reverts on both EntryPoints (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86). Deltas and claims are separate per currency address (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16), so this id cannot reach HYPE, WHYPE or USDC held for pools.

cleared.check: Can an ordinary account start a rebase of stHYPE, which would change the stHYPE balance of every holder?
cleared.result: No. Overseer.rebase reverts with AccessControlUnauthorizedAccount for role 0x5fde63b561377d1441afa201ff619faac2ff8fed70a7fbdbe7a5cb07768c0b75 when called from an unprivileged address or from the PoolManager. stHYPE.syncSupply is restricted to REBASER_ROLE (stHYPE.sol lines 392 to 396). The last rebase, at block 51,883,107, was a direct call of rebase by 0x4eb038eb501045daa520b972fcad48c429531e10. The Overseer implementation is not verified on Sourcify, so paths inside mint, burn and redeem were not read.
